c.tagline: Türkiye's modernist capital, from Atatürk's mausoleum to an ancient hilltop citadel.

taxi.fareNote: Yellow taxis are metered; Uber and BiTaksi dispatch licensed cabs. Make sure the meter (taksimetre) is running and keep small cash on hand.

emergency.note: 112 is the unified nationwide emergency number connecting to police, ambulance, and fire across Türkiye.

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing around Ulus/Kızılay; caution at night

hood_desc: The historic core on the citadel hill, home to Ankara Castle (Ankara Kalesi), the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Roman ruins, and old bazaars; best for first-timers who want the city's oldest sights and traditional atmosphere.
Ankara's bustling downtown around Kızılay Square, where the Metro and Ankaray lines meet; packed with shops, bookstores, cafes, and student life, it's the most central base for getting anywhere fast.

An upscale, leafy district of embassies, ministries, and quiet residential streets rising toward the Presidential Complex; calm and green, it suits travelers wanting a relaxed, well-to-do area away from the crowds.
The dining-and-nightlife spine of the city along Tunalı Hilmi Avenue, lined with restaurants, bars, cafes, and shopping; great for travelers who want to be where Ankara goes out in the evening.
A pleasant middle-class residential neighborhood west of the center, famous for its lively 7. Cadde (7th Street) full of casual eateries and cafes; a comfortable, local-feeling base near Anıtkabir.

water.note: Officially treated and chlorinated, but aging pipes mean bottled water is the safer choice for visitors.

transit.hours: Metro and Ankaray run roughly 06:00 to midnight; EGO city buses cover the evening with limited late-night service.
transit.note: Ankara's rail network combines the Ankaray light-metro line and the M1-M4 Metro lines, all feeding the central Kızılay interchange, backed by an extensive EGO bus network.
transit.pay: A rechargeable Ankarakart smart card is tapped on entry across the Metro, Ankaray, and buses; fares are loaded to the card and there is no on-board cash payment.

bus: Ankara Intercity Bus Terminal (AŞTİ) for coaches nationwide
train: High-speed rail (YHT) to Istanbul, Konya, Eskişehir, and Sivas from Ankara Gar

transit.m: Belko Air / HAVAŞ shuttle bus to Kızılay city center (~40-50 min)

tip.r: ~5-10% at restaurants for good service; round up taxi fares and leave small change at cafes.

food.name: Ankara tava
food.desc: The capital's namesake bake: diced lamb slow-cooked with butter and tomato, layered over rice with tail fat and finished in the oven.

places.name: Bogazici Lokantasi
places.note: Long-running Ankara lokanta of Ottoman home cooking; also known for hunkar begendi.

places.name: Goksu Lokantasi
places.note: Civil servants' canteen classic since the 1950s; daily-changing home-style trays.

places.name: Site 2 Lokantasi Abdurrahman Kucuk
places.note: Old-school meat lokanta locals name first for tandir and oven-baked lamb.

food.name: Ankara doner and Aspava
food.desc: Thinly shaved doner served Ankara-style: order one wrap and the table fills with free salad, chips, cig kofte, cacik and halva with ice cream.

places.name: Aspava houses of Bahcelievler
places.note: The street where the Aspava free-side-dish tradition is most concentrated.

places.name: Ulus doner counters
places.note: Standing-room doner shops in the old town, cheapest and busiest at lunch.

places.name: Sakarya Caddesi doner shops
places.note: Pedestrian food street packed with doner and grill counters until late.

food.name: Kuzu tandir
food.desc: Whole lamb slow-roasted in a pit oven until it falls off the bone, served on flatbread or rice; a Central Anatolian feast dish.

places.name: Site 2 Lokantasi Abdurrahman Kucuk
places.note: Widely cited as the city's benchmark for authentic kuzu tandir.

places.name: Duveroglu
places.note: Ankara institution since 1963, Gaziantep-style kitchen, lahmacun and roast meats.

places.name: Bogazici Lokantasi
places.note: Reliable roasted lamb alongside the classic Ottoman-palace repertoire.

food.name: Simit
food.desc: Sesame-crusted bread ring, crisper and thinner in Ankara than in Istanbul, eaten with tea for breakfast or on the move.

places.name: Hamamonu bakeries
places.note: Restored Ottoman quarter with wood ovens and courtyard tea gardens.

places.name: Ulus simit ovens
places.note: Old-town bakeries sell them hot from mid-morning for pocket change.

places.name: Sakarya Caddesi carts
places.note: Street carts on the food street; grab one with a glass of tea.

food.name: Beypazari kurusu
food.desc: Twice-baked dry biscuit-bread from Beypazari west of Ankara, hard and faintly sweet, dunked in tea and taken home as a souvenir.

places.name: Beypazari old town bakeries
places.note: The source town, 90 minutes west; bakeries sell it warm alongside 80-layer baklava.

places.name: Hamamonu specialty shops
places.note: Regional-produce shops in the old quarter stock it plus local tarhana and jams.

places.name: Ulus market stalls
places.note: Central Anatolian dry goods stalls sell it by weight in the old market.

food.name: Sakarya Caddesi hamsi
food.desc: Black Sea anchovies rolled in cornmeal and deep fried, eaten on plastic stools with lemon, onion and raki; a Kizilay evening ritual.

places.name: Sakarya Caddesi fish houses
places.note: Rows of simple stools and fryers; freshly fried anchovies by the plate.

places.name: Kizilay meyhanes
places.note: Back-street taverns pair the fried fish with meze and raki until late.

places.name: Bahcelievler 7. Cadde
places.note: Student-district alternative with the same fried-fish-and-raki formula.

food.name: Beypazari maden suyu
food.desc: Naturally sparkling mineral water from Beypazari, bottled since 1957 and the default drink with a heavy Ankara meat meal.

places.name: Kizilay lokantas
places.note: Every home-cooking lokanta keeps it cold; order it with tandir or tava.

places.name: Beypazari town springs
places.note: Visit the source town for the springs plus its market of local produce.

places.name: Hamamonu tea gardens
places.note: Courtyard cafes serve it plain or as a lemon-and-mint gazoz.

food.name: Turkish coffee and tea
food.desc: Thick coffee cooked in sand or copper and endless tulip glasses of tea, taken in Ankara's restored Ottoman courtyards.

places.name: Hamamonu courtyard cafes
places.note: Restored 19th-century houses with garden tables; the nicest place to linger.

places.name: Ankara Castle terraces
places.note: Rooftop tea houses inside the citadel walls with views over the whole city.

places.name: Kugulu Park cafes
places.note: Park-side cafes popular with locals for afternoon coffee under the trees.

landmarks: Anıtkabir
The monumental hilltop mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, founder of the Turkish Republic, is Ankara's most solemn and grand architectural icon.
Ankara Castle (Ankara Kalesi)
This ancient hilltop citadel with its Roman-Byzantine-Ottoman walls offers sweeping panoramic views over the old city and is Ankara's most photographed skyline feature.
Kocatepe Mosque
Turkey's largest mosque, with its soaring Ottoman-style domes and minarets, dominates Ankara's skyline and dazzles at night when illuminated.
Temple of Augustus and Rome
A remarkably preserved 2,000-year-old Roman temple bearing the famous inscribed 'Res Gestae' of Emperor Augustus, standing right in the heart of the old city.
Museum of Anatolian Civilizations
A UNESCO-honored, award-winning museum housing one of the world's finest collections of Hittite and ancient Anatolian artifacts inside a restored Ottoman bedesten.
Atakule Tower
This distinctive 125-meter observation tower with a glass-domed top is a beloved modern landmark offering 360-degree views of the capital.
Roman Baths of Ankara
The evocative ruins of an ancient Roman bathing complex, with its rows of surviving columns, transport visitors back to Ankara's days as Roman Ancyra.
Column of Julian
A slender 15-meter Roman column erected to honor Emperor Julian's visit in 362 AD, standing as a striking solitary monument near Ulus Square.
Hacı Bayram Mosque
A beloved 15th-century mosque built beside the Temple of Augustus, revered as the spiritual heart of old Ankara and a pilgrimage site for Hacı Bayram Veli's tomb.
Ethnography Museum of Ankara
This elegant white marble building displays rich Anatolian folk-art and Ottoman-era artifacts and once held Atatürk's temporary tomb.

train.note: No international trains leave Ankara - the old Trans-Asia Express to Tehran now starts from Van, and the Balkan sleepers run from Istanbul's Halkali. Ankara Gar is the hub of the YHT high-speed network, reaching Istanbul in about 4h30, Konya in 1h45 and Sivas in around 5 hours. Book on the TCDD e-bilet site, which opens 15 days ahead - YHT seats on Friday and Sunday sell out quickly.

intl.op: Vardar Turizm and other Turkish carriers — tickets at the Ankara AŞTİ terminal

bus.note: Everything leaves from AŞTİ, the vast terminal west of the centre on the Ankaray light-rail line. Kamil Koç (https://www.kamilkoc.com.tr/) and Pamukkale (https://www.pamukkale.com.tr/) run the main domestic routes, and the aggregator obilet (https://www.obilet.com/en/) lists every operator in one place. International coaches take a long time at the land borders - carry your passport and check visa rules for Iran and Georgia.

ferry.note: Ankara sits on the central Anatolian plateau with no coast and no navigable river, so there are no ferries of any kind.

half.name: Beypazarı
half.blurb: Small town of cobblestone streets and preserved Ottoman houses, known for its silverwork and carrot fields.

half.name: Kızılcahamam
half.blurb: Forested spa town with thermal hot springs and long hiking trails through Soğuksu National Park.

full.name: Hattusas
full.blurb: Ruined capital of the ancient Hittite Empire, a UNESCO site with monumental gates and rock-cut sanctuaries.

full.name: Safranbolu
full.blurb: UNESCO-listed Ottoman town of timber houses, cobbled lanes, and historic bathhouses in the Black Sea foothills.
